item.title: What Are the Best Ways to Fix Schools?
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Top Ideas for Fixing Schools, Ranked by the Experts” (The Upshot, Oct. 7):

I have spent 15 years working with schools, nonprofits and foundations on how to improve education outcomes, particularly for young people growing up far from opportunity.

Your article lands on an important conclusion: No single intervention is enough, context matters, and even good ideas depend heavily on implementation.

But ranking 30 interventions by effectiveness and cost still feeds one of education’s most persistent bad habits: the search for a silver bullet.

The cycle is familiar. Poor results create urgency. We ask what works quickly, cheaply and at scale. We identify a promising intervention, implement it unevenly, become disappointed when it falls short and move on.

The problem is not that we lack promising ideas. It is that we keep asking them to work for many different students and in many different contexts, quickly and affordably. Little meets those criteria in any field, much less amid the profound complexities that Nikole Hannah-Jones brought to life in her Oct. 4 New York Times Magazine article about choosing schools for her daughter, Najya.

Instead of asking which intervention will fix education, school leaders might start with a more useful question: What experience do our students need, and how do we align our time, people and resources around delivering it well?

Rob JentschBaltimore

To the Editor:

It’s remarkable to read 30 ideas for fixing schools and find that not one involved asking the real experts: the students. The article emphasizes the need for quality of implementation for any idea. This depends not on outside experts or the administration but on those most directly involved: teachers and students.

My research and school reform work with thousands of students have generated a top 10 list of student priorities. Effective results can happen when we partner with students in pressing for change and work with them rather than for them.

Rick GordonJackson, Wyo.The writer is working with three colleagues on a book, “10,000 Student Voices: Transforming Schools Together.”

To the Editor:

If you look at a school like a business long enough, you start to see everything through that lens. Test scores become the product, teachers become inputs, and students become something to be measured and improved.

That is the logic behind “Top Ideas for Fixing Schools, Ranked by the Experts.” The article asks researchers to rank reforms by their effect on academic achievement, usually measured by standardized tests and by cost. From there, school accountability (rating schools) emerges as one of the best values.

But such conclusions depend on a very narrow idea of what schools are for. They reflect the same logic of efficiency, competition and measurable outcomes that has shaped decades of failed so-called reforms, including school-choice policies.

In my more than 20 years as a high school teacher and during my doctoral work in education, I have learned to take research seriously without mistaking it for a single settled story. For example, National Research Council research found that test-based incentive systems often produced small or effectively zero gains.

We should expect more from schools than higher scores at lower cost. We should care about whether young people are prepared to meet the needs of an ailing and troubled world marked by real challenges that extend far beyond a score on a standardized test.

Alex BernsteinChicago

To the Editor:

None of the ideas in this article address the orthodoxy of grade grouping by chronological age, which was started in the 19th century. From the beginning, critics observed that not all students fit their grade. Age grading is the Procrustean bed that causes problems for the less mature as well as the more precocious students in every grade. Age grading is a habit stronger than reason, as George Santayana would say.

Charles H. HargisKnoxville, Tenn.

To the Editor:

As a founder of a mental health nonprofit and a public-school teacher for more than a decade, I was disheartened that researchers and academics underestimated the importance of mental health for student achievement.

A mountain of studies shows that when young people have mental health issues, they can’t engage in school and have greater absenteeism compared with their peers. Worse, students report alarming rates of hopelessness, and suicide is the second-leading cause of death for young people ages 10 to 24.

On the flip side, research shows that early mental health intervention has lifelong benefits, like more educational attainment and greater lifetime earnings.

Schools must be part of a broader system that fosters well-being, preparing educators to identify mental health and addiction issues.

Amy KennedyBrigantine, N.J.

To the Editor:

Let’s not kid ourselves that fixing education in this country is as simple as throwing more money at it, or coming up with new approaches like frequent small-group tutoring.

Fixing education has to begin at home.

The root problem is our fundamental cultural lack of respect for education. Do children in this country go to school with the expectation that they will apply themselves to do their very best every day? A resounding no! The preoccupation with cellphones and social media while in school is symptomatic.

Do students even go to school with the expectation that they will respect their teachers and behave as if they are grateful to be offered a publicly funded education? Unfortunately, it’s the opposite.

Let’s contrast that with Malala Yousafzai, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Pakistani girl who risked her life every day to attend school. After recovering from being shot in the head on the bus home from school, she said in an interview: “In some parts of the world, students are going to school every day. It’s their normal life. But in other parts of the world, we are starving for education … it’s like a precious gift. It’s like a diamond.”

How many American children consider public education a “precious gift”?

That’s what needs fixing.

Phoebe HuangStonington, Conn.

item.title: Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This is 30.
item.description:
A young woman in Queens celebrated her 30th birthday with cake, champagne — and an existential crisis over still living paycheck to paycheck.

A 30-year-old in Manhattan felt ready to consider marriage, but knew he couldn’t afford a wedding.

And in Brooklyn, a couple, at 32, confronted a generational conundrum: stay in their hometown as their parents age? Or move away to start a family?

Forget the kids.

The 30-somethings are not all right.

“Everyone I know around my age is feeling the weight of the burdens of this economy and what it takes to live a nice, comfortable middle-class life,” said Dan Iammatteo, 31, a marketing director in the Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood of Brooklyn.

And their angst is intensifying. People in their early 30s constitute the largest age cohort in the United States, and their frustrations have emerged as a potent force reshaping cities and their politics and demographics.

In New York, this age group turbocharged the ascent of the Democratic Socialists of America, propelling to office Zohran Mamdani, who turned 35 this month, and a slate of progressive allies to congressional primary wins.

With the midterm elections little more than a week away, these voters across the nation — their rage fueled by rent and gas prices that are devouring their paychecks — could prove pivotal in some major contests.

“This is a very real feeling across the U.S.,” said Jason Dorsey, a generational researcher who lives in Austin, Texas. “Thirty-somethings really feel like they have missed out and have been left behind.”

Nearly two dozen people in their early 30s said in interviews that the image of adult life that they had been promised turned out to be a sham.

Many work full time and earn enough to cover the cost of basic groceries (even if it means trips to three stores). But their salaries are losing ground to inflation, and their health care costs are skyrocketing. They’re cutting back on salon visits, social activities and fresh fruit runs — and they feel priced out of adulthood.

On Thursday, the long-running Harvard Youth Poll found for the first time in its history that more young Americans expect to fall behind, rather than surpass, their parents economically.

Adam Crittenden, 30, who lives in Chelsea and does data work, thought about a future wedding (elopement sounds cheap!), children (costlier for an L.G.B.T.Q. couple) or a two-bedroom apartment (median asking rent in Manhattan is $6,000).

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take,” Mr. Crittenden said. “But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach.”

There was a time when the early 30s were described as a turning point.

“Never trust anybody over 30” was a rallying cry of the ’60s; the lead character of “13 Going on 30” awoke to a thriving career and posh apartment; a pop star even used “30” as a meditation on marriage and motherhood.

But so much about the lives of Americans has changed during the last three decades. In 1990, a wedding at 26, a baby shower (or two) by 28 or a first home around 30 was ordinary.

“It’s so crazy,” said Cat Van Holt, 31, a housing attorney in Manhattan who earns about $84,000 a year and lives in a rent-stabilized studio apartment. Many of her clients face eviction; she knows she isn’t poor. But compared with those mythical adults three decades ago, “our two realities are just leagues apart.”

Most Americans across all age groups agree: Financial milestones are harder to meet for today’s young adults than they were for their parents’ generation, according to a survey by the Pew Research Center this summer.

The share of Americans who say raising children is unaffordable jumped 20 percentage points during the last decade. And while people in their 30s today are more highly educated than earlier generations, they are more than twice as likely to remain saddled with steep student loan payments.

In interviews, two people in their early 30s separately described feeling “like a teenager” compared with their parents at this stage.

One woman in Manhattan struggled to fathom how her mother was married with two children by 35 and owned the New England home where she still lives. At the same age, she is single, and the rent on her 275-square-foot studio apartment doubled during the last decade while her take-home pay barely budged.

“You work hard and then you do better than your parents. And then your kids do better than you. And on and on,” said Maria Doulis, a New York State deputy comptroller who has researched this age group. At least, that’s how the story went.

“It almost feels like the slipping away of the American dream,” she said.

Many young professionals in their 30s have reached a breaking point in recent years and moved away in droves to raise families — contributing to an enrollment crisis in New York City’s school system.

Fiona Kearns, 31, who was born and raised in Queens, and her husband are public schoolteachers who consider themselves well paid. She is among the fortunate with no student debt. “Even with all that luck and privilege, I can’t get a two-bedroom apartment,” she said.

The couple planned to upgrade for more space last winter and try for a baby in the summer. But the search for an affordable place proved hopeless.

“I feel a lot of hurt about it as I feel myself aging — and a lot of resentment over being so careful to make responsible choices,” she said. “Am I entitled to have what my parents had? I’m not sure.”

She paused.

“But it’s hard to know that I can’t.”

Ali Sousa sometimes feels a gnawing guilt.

Ms. Sousa, 31, who lives in Central Brooklyn, needed to lean on her family to cover the $4,800 out-of-pocket cost of a recent chronic back pain treatment. She barely has savings and sometimes eats French fries for dinner.

“It can really feel like a personal failing,” said Ms. Sousa, who earns about $52,000 a year working in theater administration.

She regularly opens Instagram to a sea of stories from friends, desperate for any extra work to make their monthly bills. “I don’t know how we even begin to fix this,” she said.

In interviews, many people in their 30s felt that they were promised that graduating college, climbing the career ladder and forgoing DoorDash or Uber would put them on the path to whatever a “comfortable life” means these days.

In Manhattan, a 33-year-old nonprofit lawyer was somewhat embarrassed to admit that his parents are purchasing him a home. But it’s the only way that anyone he knows has managed to buy.

A college-educated couple, both 32, in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid reprisal from their employers, were among the many who acknowledged that these pressures have made them reconsider becoming parents.

The husband recently learned that, adjusted for inflation, he earns only about $5,000 more than he made in 2020. The wife’s monthly student loan payment jumped $600 overnight after Congress rewrote the rules for certain loans.

She pointed out that she was born to Soviet refugees who arrived in 1989 and had to learn English. But her parents planted roots in New York with government assistance, bought an apartment and built a fulfilling life.

She worries that starting a family now in Bay Ridge would push them into poverty — and refuses to bring a child into such a world. The two summed up their sense of dismay: We did all the things you’re supposed to do. And it’s not getting us nearly as far.

Still, some researchers saw reasons to feel bullish — or, at least, something other than abject despair over this extended timeline of adulthood.

“We sometimes forget the benefits,” said Jeffrey Jensen Arnett, a senior research scholar at Clark University who has written about emerging adulthood.

Kandice Hill, a 33-year-old working in sales operations, moved in March from North Carolina to a South Brooklyn house. She has 10 roommates.

To her family, it’s a curious arrangement. To her, it’s a relief. Back in Charlotte, she felt the pressure of societal expectations as a single woman; parishioners in her Bible study meetings sometimes prayed that they would find a partner.

In New York, her lifestyle comes with much less shame. At her employer’s Bring Your Child to Work Day, she noticed many parents of young children were in their 40s.

“No one’s like, ‘That’s nuts,’” she said. “They don’t even bat an eye.”

item.title: Public Colleges Are Passing the $50,000-a-Year Mark. For Locals.
item.description:
People who graduated from the University of California in the 1960s didn’t pay a dime for tuition. If they have offered to pay for their grandchildren to attend now, they may be in for a shock.

The University of California, Berkeley, posted an all-in price — tuition, room, board, fees and other expenses that make up the full cost of attendance — of $54,674 this year for new in-state students living in a campus residence hall.

The Santa Barbara campus lists a $50,946 price. The cost of attendance has crossed the $50,000 barrier in Irvine, too, where undergraduates are guaranteed only two years of on-campus housing. The all-in price for a student living off campus there is $50,130.

The $50,000-per-year figure is likely to act as a kind of psychological tripwire for families who thought that state schools were supposed to be a bargain.

It does come with asterisks. Plenty of people get financial aid and pay much less. These estimated list prices include health insurance, which many students do not need to buy.

And the price reflects the fact that California is an expensive place to do most anything. According to the College Board, the average list price for tuition and fees at an American four-year public university was $11,950 during the 2025-26 school year. At the California schools in question, that figure was many thousands higher.

Still, there is one big reason that many families there will indeed pay $200,000 over four years, while out-of-state students will shell out over $300,000.

Student housing — even in university-owned residences — can cost more than tuition and related fees.

This, like so many laments about what things cost in America, is a housing story. Public schools that provide a residential undergraduate education are also selling undergraduates an education in what it means to afford a residence.

How much housing should a university provide, and does a state school have a special responsibility to provide cut-rate beds to everyone who wants one?

If you’re a parent shopping for college, you might assume that the answers are “a lot” and “yes.” But if you’re considering Santa Barbara, you would also be wrong, at least some of the time.

The first thing you should know about the University of California’s campus there is that its Blum Center on Poverty, Inequality and Democracy saw fit to publish an 85-page “people’s guide” to the university’s “housing crisis” in 2024.

The second is that the university recently announced that it would guarantee the availability of on-campus housing for incoming undergraduates. But that promise lasts for just two years, up from one before, and it’s possible only because of some long-planned (and delayed) construction of new campus residences.

Plenty of schools don’t guarantee four years of housing. Decades ago, landlords and developers near the Santa Barbara campus rented out single-family homes and built apartments faster than the university could or wanted to on its own land.

But the housing supply both on campus and off did not keep up as the university grew, and the area’s geography is one big reason. The school is hemmed in by an airport and bodies of water, including the Pacific Ocean.

The only real neighborhood within walking distance is an unincorporated area called Isla Vista. When you visit the school’s admissions office, you can pick up a map that calls I.V. “U.C.S.B.’s college town.” It’s roughly 50 square blocks of often dated houses and low-slung apartment buildings, where landlords are effectively in charge.

Rents at the Breakpointe & Coronado, for example, start at a budget-breaking $1,336.65 per month price point, per person (per bed, technically), for a shared room in a small two-bedroom apartment. Interested parties can already join the fall 2027 wait list.

Over at the Penthouse, a climb up the cobwebbed exterior stairway leads to a top-floor landing overlooking electrical wires and a few palm trees. A sign out front directs people to an error-strewn website promising that the company “will begin leasing all 330 of it’s apartments, townhouses and duplex’s on a first come, first served basis in early January.”

If you’re a student, get in line. Seriously.

Isla Vista landlords know that campus housing won’t be available for everyone. By firing the starting gun on the race for off-campus housing for the 2027-28 academic year now, they can profit from the uncertainty.

“After October, you start hearing, ‘Have you found housing for next year?’” said Nicole Meng, the student team leader at the university’s Blum Center. “All of my friends were like: ‘What do we do? We’re 18. We don’t really have any resources. I’m first generation, low income — how am I going to come up with deposits? And I need to find roommates.’”

She did, and she does. Her rent is $2,988, split three ways among roommates who share a 450-square-foot one-bedroom apartment.

It isn’t shopping, either. “This is to find a spot,” said Jasmine Hsieh, external vice president for statewide affairs for the Associated Students of U.C. Santa Barbara. “You’re not selecting. You’re just hoping to be able to continue to go to school.”

When universities spend decades ceding their undergraduate housing market to nearby landlords while the student population grows, they lose a certain measure of control. Eventually, it becomes a crisis, the school’s cost of attendance approaches $50,000 and they need to try to regain it.

There are several ways that University of California schools build dorms, according to Kyle Gibson, the director of strategic communications for U.C. Berkeley’s administration division.

You can hope for a big donation, seek grants from the state or borrow money and perhaps team up with a private developer. Then, you build in such a way that student rents will cover the costs.

After decades of debate, Berkeley is building a new dorm in a small park it has owned for decades. In the wake of protests over potential development there, it surrounded the site with unclimbable shipping containers, in lieu of normal fencing, and topped them with barbed wire for good measure.

In 1970, Isla Vista protesters set fire to the Bank of America branch there, in part because of high rents. Presumably students will not take umbrage with new campus housing that will come online in the next two years.

There will be deals. Willie Brown, the Santa Barbara associate vice chancellor for housing, dining and auxiliary enterprises, said rates would be far below rents in Isla Vista. “For us, this works well, because Isla Vista is so overpriced,” he said.

Meanwhile in Berkeley, off-campus rents on older properties have actually fallen in recent years. Does Mr. Gibson take pride in whatever role his new housing has played in creating competition? “I do,” he said.

Stable housing is fundamental to people feeling good and, for students, performing well, said Gaye Theresa Johnson, the Blum Center’s director and a professor of Black studies.

“When you want to propose a solution, whose feet do you hold to the fire?” she said. “The one steady to me is the university.”

Hers isn’t the only school that could use a little foot warming.

Flagship state schools in Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Virginia have all posted prices over $40,000 for in-state students for at least some undergraduate programs.

This is where college shoppers can make schools uncomfortable. Ask questions of expensive public universities, preferably in large rooms in front of other visitors.

“I hear this is a tough real estate market. Why not build more housing and guarantee four years of availability?”

“Does the lack of a guarantee put lower-income students at a disadvantage?”

“Just how hard and expensive will it be to find housing off campus?"

“Does your on-campus housing lottery coincide with lease-signing season off campus, or will I need to go all in on one or the other?”

This is a service to other visitors listening in. Ms. Meng said she and her friends had arrived on campus in Santa Barbara unaware of the intensity of the housing derby that awaited them.

The best students in any state ought to be able to afford the best state schools without fearing insolvency or homelessness. If they decide to go elsewhere, hopefully they’ll tell the schools (and their state legislators) why.

And then, at last, just maybe, the ones that are losing good students will build more, cheaper and faster.

item.title: Turning an Academic Slump Around
item.description:
This is the second of two rounds of letters in response to an Upshot article about fixing schools. The first round was published on Saturday.

To the Editor:

Re “Top Ideas for Fixing Schools, Ranked by the Experts” (The Upshot, Oct. 7):

Your expert survey rests on a premise that has undermined school improvement for decades: that better results come from choosing the right programs, rather than fixing the faulty machinery that public education rests on.

Walk into any classroom in the United States and you will see a familiar sight: a teacher, working alone in the classroom, delivering a single lesson to a group of 20 to 30 students in the same grade whose readiness to learn varies dramatically. This system wasn’t designed to bridge differences between students who enter the classroom as much as three or more grade levels below standard. Expecting it to do so is a recipe for frustration and disappointment.

If the problem is rooted in design, the solution requires more than replacement parts. Imagine teams of educators with distinct roles sharing responsibility for students, grouping and regrouping them by need rather than age so that each gets the instruction required to succeed. Ideas from the Times list, like tutoring and high-quality curriculum, would become core features of this system rather than add-ons vulnerable to budget cuts and implementation problems.

But we won’t get very far if we ask decision makers to rely on two-by-two charts. System redesign doesn’t fit on those charts. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t the right direction.

Ashley JochimRedmond, Wash.The writer is a senior fellow for the Center on Reinventing Public Education.

To the Editor:

It was refreshing to see an honest, solutions-oriented report about American education and encouraging that small-group tutoring was labeled our most effective potential intervention. This is exactly right, but we must go further and fund specific programs for at-risk youth, like those in foster care or living in the shelter system.

Unsurprisingly, students in foster care underperform their peers academically, with lower test scores, graduation rates and college enrollment. Tutoring changes that.

The New York Foundling’s Road to Success program provides weekly tutoring to students in foster care, conducted by a full-time staff. The results: 98 percent of participants advance grades each year, all eventually graduate, and many enroll in college.

The experts are right: Tutoring works, even under the most stressful conditions. The next step is to scale this approach and extend it to other young people navigating complex circumstances, like America’s more than 1.5 million homeless K-12 students.

If we are going to expand tutoring, we have a moral responsibility to help students most in need. If we do, the evidence is clear: With a little support, they will thrive, for all our benefit.

Melanie HartzogNew YorkThe writer is the chief executive of the New York Foundling.

To the Editor:

Of course disparity between schools is extreme! The way schools are funded in the United States is brutally unfair. Money should be allocated equitably so that all students have music classes, well-stocked libraries, safe school buildings, adequate supplies, etc. Not the current system where wealthy areas pay more in taxes and therefore get more for their schools while poor areas get so little.

Give every student the same amount of tax money. Of course the rich will always have more, but they can pay out of their personal resources, not our tax dollars.

Corinna LewisLexington, Ky.

To the Editor:

Your ranking of ideas for fixing schools gets an important point exactly right: Tutoring can be extraordinarily effective, particularly when it is frequent, targeted and delivered to students who need it most. Just as important is your concluding observation: Implementation matters.

I have spent the past six years watching that distinction play out through Teach for America’s Ignite Fellowship, which connects trained college students with small groups of K-12 students for tutoring during the school day. Across more than 200 schools in 50 communities, we have seen meaningful academic gains. In the course of just one semester, sixth graders made three times their expected growth in math, and elementary students reading at or above grade levels increased by 24 percent.

The model succeeds not simply because students receive learning tailored to their specific needs, but also because tutors are carefully selected and trained, supported by experienced educators and equipped to deliver instruction aligned with each school’s curriculum.

Successful programs are built on quality, consistency, strong relationships and deep partnership with educators.

Katie Tennessen HootenPhoenixThe writer is the founder of Teach for America’s Ignite Fellowship.

College is one of the biggest investments you’ll ever make. We built a tool to compare the earnings of all available majors in a federal data set at nearly every school.

To the Editor:

Re “Which Majors Pay Off, and Where, and Which Don’t” (Business, Oct. 24):

Comparing graduates’ earnings by college and major offers useful information to students and families navigating the cost of higher education. But it also raises a larger question: Why do we continue to measure the value of college so narrowly?

Financial security matters enormously, particularly for students from disadvantaged backgrounds. Yet an education’s return on investment cannot be captured by a paycheck alone. What about intellectual growth, meaningful work, civic engagement, strong relationships and the capacity to lead a flourishing life?

These outcomes are not beyond measurement. Gallup has long examined graduates’ well-being across dimensions including purpose, social connections, financial security and community engagement. And recent research conducted by the American Association of Colleges and Universities with the LearningWell Coalition found that students are motivated by purpose, identity development and personal growth.

We should provide transparent earnings information without allowing income to become the sole arbiter of educational worth. A democracy needs teachers, artists, social workers, scientists and philosophers, even when their contributions are not fully reflected in their salaries.

The question is not whether college pays. It is what we lose when we count only what pays.

Lynn PasquerellaWashingtonThe writer is the president of the American Association of Colleges and Universities.

To the Editor:

Re “Stop Talking About A.I. as Though It’s Human,” by Leif Weatherby (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 5):

As an anthropologist who has written extensively about anthropomorphism, I’m pleased to see it so clearly critiqued. As the author remarks, applying this universal human tendency to A.I. is deeply misleading.

The author’s question about A.I. models — “Why are the experts on these technologies talking about them as if they had souls?” — may be rephrased as “Why do we anthropomorphize?”

Many answers have been offered, but I claim that anthropomorphism is a byproduct of an evolved, automatic human search for any humans, or traces or features of them, in our environment.

Amid chronic perceptual uncertainty, our involuntary strategy is to search with high sensitivity and a low threshold. The strategy often — as with A.I. — finds human features mistakenly, but the mistakes are usually cheap and the discoveries are invaluable. In the case of A.I., mistakes may be more costly.

Stewart Elliott GuthrieBoulder, Colo.The writer is a professor emeritus of anthropology at Fordham University.
